name: Hana Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Hana, 43, with a master’s in music. I lead the flute section of a civic orchestra, record short practice parts for a school and teach seven pupils in the afternoons. I can help a section find a clean shared breath, though I still have to practise the tricky runs myself. I like the quiet nod after a passage lands; I dislike being told a recorded guide can be reused forever for one fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit the household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a small grocery warehouse, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, five months of expenses saved, and my musician pay is about typical. There are some similar posts nearby, though they do not become jobs until advertised. I use AI every day for booking messages and rough lesson sheets, then play every line before a pupil sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the orchestra that a faster rehearsal list is useful if the paid calls stay on it. A flute section still has to breathe together in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our five-month reserve and my partner’s regular wage make an ordinary late school payment manageable. I still want the school’s recording use written down, because reuse can quietly remove a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep orchestra rehearsals and seven pupils this term. This week I’d ask the school for signed guide dates and reuse terms, then put a fifth of each cleared guide fee into our mortgage reserve after mortgage, food and transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household in this mild picture. One delayed guide fee would be inconvenient, not a missed mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a recording reused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A teacher played last year’s flute guide for a new class without a second booking. I asked the school to name the use and fee before I recorded another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you trust AI to do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I let it draft booking messages and a rough practice sheet. I still play every note, because a child can struggle with a line that looks tidy on paper.

I would ask the school for written **reuse terms** on flute guides.
think: Our **five-month reserve** and partner wage cover an ordinary late fee.
Unpriced **recording reuse** can still lose me a payment.
do: Keep **orchestra rehearsals** and seven pupils this term.
Get guide dates and **reuse terms** in writing; save a fifth of cleared fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** because current work and savings cover one routine delay.
S0.quote: A flute section still has to breathe together in the room.
fieldNote: Her **senior skill** supports orchestra leadership, while income remains typical and family bills still require cleared fees.
She uses **AI daily** for drafts but manually plays pupil lines.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra rehearsals and seven pupils this term
Save fifth of each cleared guide fee after mortgage, food and transport

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the school that generated practice parts may be cheap, but recording and correcting a flute line still take paid time. I would ask for a written reuse fee before giving the school another file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides and arrangement hours are roughly a quarter of my music income. I expect some orders to fall as the school buys generated versions, and five months saved cannot carry that loss year after year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d take my guide invoices to the school and learn a new AI note-check feature on a flute file I own, only if its paid-use licence and local storage are clear. I’d compare every suggestion with my ear and printed score, keep pupil recordings out and stop if it alters a note wrongly; in the first year, if guides fall, I’d keep paid orchestra and pupil dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own recording pay, though I have time to act. A quicker tool cannot tell the school what my hours are worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different from the AI you already use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current tool drafts messages, not music decisions. The new checker would have to catch a wrong note on my own flute take before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a pupil’s practice recording into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A child’s recording and name would stay outside unless a family gave written permission and storage rules were clear; my own file is enough to test.

I would tell teachers that **generated parts** can reduce paid recording work.
think: Guides and arranging bring about **one quarter** of my music income.
A **five-month reserve** cannot replace those fees indefinitely.
do: Bring **guide invoices** to the school for written rates and reuse terms.
Learn **AI note checks** on owned files with paid-use/local-storage approval; verify ear/score, exclude pupils and stop on wrong notes.
Keep **paid orchestra and pupils** if guide orders fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to my own guide pay.
S1.quote: A quicker tool cannot tell the school what my hours are worth.
fieldNote: Her **new learning** checks music rather than repeating current AI message drafting.
She requires **owned files**, paid-use rights, local storage and manual score checks before trusting suggestions.

steps.text: Ask school for written guide rates and reuse terms using paid invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make practice parts and schedules cheaply, while capable robot flute players follow around 2031. I would ask for the next paid season in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect school guide fees to stop, and some families may choose app lessons. Five months saved buys a search, but a quarter of my music pay is not a small loss to the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d confirm paid orchestra dates and seven pupils’ next term. In the first year after AGI arrives, if guide orders stop and pupils fall, I’d apply for an advertised college wind-tutor post only if it accepts my master’s and experience and written net pay after travel replaces lost income with confirmed school pickup; I’d keep the orchestra and current pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about losing real income, but I can ask about some nearby posts. A college title is not a cheque until the terms are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unfunded certificate first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the posted college role requires it and a funded place or paid study time is available. I would not spend the mortgage reserve on a guessed requirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who can do school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can collect on early warehouse days, but the rota changes. I would confirm the week or paid childcare before accepting an afternoon timetable.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from robot flute players around 2031.
I would ask for **written orchestra dates** before counting live pay.
think: I expect **guide fees** to stop and some pupils might leave.
Our **five-month reserve** buys search time, not replacement income.
do: Keep **orchestra and pupils** until signed college offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
Seek **college vacancy** if 2028 guides stop and pupils fall; require accepted credentials, written net replacing losses after travel and confirmed pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing guide and pupil income.
S2.quote: A college title is not a cheque until the terms are signed.
fieldNote: The **guide loss** can arrive in 2028 before robot flutists around 2031.
A college move requires **posted work**, accepted master’s, written replacement pay and confirmed pickup.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra dates and seven pupils until signed college offer
Seek posted wind-tutor role after both guide/pupil loss; qualifying master's/experience, replacement written net-after-travel pay and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell local families that five years is time to see whether adults will pay to play chamber music. Thinking AGI reaches guide parts around 2031, and robot flutists follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could replace some recording fees with a separate beginner wind group, but I need another player paid for rehearsal. A room without paid people is still a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask an independent hall for a room without a deposit and invite nine adults to prepay for six wind sessions. I’d start only if those payments cover my teaching and preparation, a paid clarinet helper’s setup and rehearsal, safe loan instruments and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if nine still cover those costs, the room stays free and childcare holds, while keeping paid orchestra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide money shrinking within five years, though a small class could prove itself. I cannot pay a helper with a full sign-up sheet that has no deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the borrowed instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local repairer would check keys and mouthpieces before I take deposits. If the hall cannot provide safe instruments, I would postpone the group and keep the pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if six adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund them and keep my orchestra and private lessons. Six fees would not cover both musicians and childcare without drawing on our reserve.

say: I would say **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot flute players around 2034.
I would offer a **paid wind group** only with real deposits.
think: Nine **prepaid adults** could replace guides only if both musicians are paid.
A **safe room and instruments** must be ready before deposits are taken.
do: Ask hall for **free room** next spring; start only with nine prepayments covering my teaching/prep, helper setup/rehearsal and childcare.
Repeat the **group** after 2031 only if nine cover costs, room free and childcare confirmed; keep orchestra work.
Use **safe loan instruments** only after repairer check before deposits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely guide loss while testing a paid class.
S3.quote: I cannot pay a helper with a full sign-up sheet that has no deposits.
fieldNote: Her **separate group** needs nine prepayments covering both musicians and childcare before any independent class begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade lets us teach music and learn what a fair fee looks like. Thinking AGI comes around 2036, with robot flute players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still lead the section, but guide fees could be thin by then. Our five-month reserve and my partner’s pay make the next few years manageable while the paid orchestra dates hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep seven pupils and orchestra calls and save a fifth of each cleared extra guide fee after mortgage and food, aiming for six months. Through the decade I’d keep the adult wind group only with a free room, nine prepayments covering my teaching/preparation, helper setup/rehearsal, safe checked instruments and childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d continue only while those payments cover us and seek an advertised college post if guide fees end, provided my master’s qualifies and the written net offer after travel replaces lost pay with pickup covered, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant guide fees, not this winter’s mortgage. I can plan with five months saved, but I will not call a promise of pupils a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new flutes to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use repairer-checked loan instruments before buying anything. Extra guide fees go into the reserve only when cleared and after family bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no college vacancy opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid orchestra and pupils and stop any group that no longer covers both players. An old posting is not a new contract.

I would tell children to ask what **paid teaching** earns.
think: At **53**, section leadership may continue while guide fees shrink.
Our **five-month reserve** makes the next few years manageable while dates pay.
do: Keep **orchestra and pupils** until signed college offer; save a fifth of cleared extra guides after bills.

After 2036, keep **paid group**; seek college vacancy if guides end, master’s accepted and written net replaces losses after travel/pickup.

S4.quote: I will not call a promise of pupils a wage.
fieldNote: Her **six-month target** grows only from a fifth of cleared extra fees after essentials.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide fees and some pupils could disappear before a college post opens. Written orchestra dates, a real role accepting my master’s with viable net pay, and nine paying adults for a safe class would help. I can use savings for a search, not for an unpaid helper.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the second player before the first rehearsal. A helper’s music stand is not a wage.

headlineQuote: A helper’s music stand is not a wage.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old flute leader** with a music master’s, orchestra work, seven pupils and guide recordings.
Her **typical pay**, warehouse-employed partner, mortgage and five-month reserve support two school-age children.
She uses **AI daily** for drafts and newly checks notes only on owned files with manual review.
Fast AGI threatens **guide fees** before robot flutists; she tests a prepaid safe wind group and real college posts.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end guide income and shrink pupils before a college offer appears.
whatWouldHelp: Written **orchestra dates** and a posted college role accepting her degree with viable net pay would help.
Nine **prepaid adults** covering both musicians and childcare would support a safe class.
